name: Lingual braces
lead: Lingual braces are fixed orthodontic appliances bonded to the tongue-facing (inner) surfaces of the teeth rather than the outer surfaces, so that they are largely hidden from view. [1]

They are used for the same purposes as conventional braces, such as straightening teeth and correcting bite problems. Encyclopedic accounts and a 2016 systematic review summarised there report that lingual appliances are associated with more tongue pain, harder oral hygiene and more speech and eating difficulty than labial braces, and that mechanical finishing is harder because the brackets sit closer together. [1]

In looksmaxxing communities, braces in general are discussed mainly in terms of whether they improve the smile or can alter facial structure; lingual braces as a separate topic appear far less often than discussion of braces overall. [2][3]

paras: Lingual braces consist of brackets and wires attached to the back of the teeth. Their principal advantage is that they are almost invisible in ordinary view, compared with brackets on the cheek-facing side. [1] Modern systems may use customised brackets made from digital scans, whereas early designs used prefabricated brackets. [1]

Craven Kurz, working with Jim Mulick at the UCLA School of Dentistry, developed the first lingual appliance in 1975 and 1976 and treated the first patient in Beverly Hills in 1976, after the patient asked for braces without visible metal. Kurz filed a patent that year, and the manufacturer Ormco produced the first brackets in 1979. [1]

Interest declined around 1989 after clinicians reported difficulties and returned from about 2008 as laboratory techniques and digital technology improved. Professional societies for lingual orthodontics formed in France, the United States, Europe and the United Kingdom between 1986 and 2003. [1]
Reported advantages are appearance during treatment and fewer visible decalcification marks on the outer tooth surfaces, although poor hygiene can still produce white spot lesions. [1]

Reported disadvantages include tongue irritation, speech difficulty and a higher rate of bracket breakage, particularly with earlier designs. Patients are typically told irritation and speech effects improve over a few weeks. Brackets are closer together than on labial braces, which can make some finishing movements more difficult. [1]

A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis, as summarised by Wikipedia, found more tongue pain, harder oral hygiene and more speech and eating difficulties with lingual braces than with labial braces. [1] A 2005 German study of 40 women, also summarised there, reported fewer tongue problems with customised brackets than with prefabricated ones, but its measures were subjective. [1]

Among broader orthodontic research, a randomised trial of 66 adults compared Invisalign aligners with traditional fixed appliances on finished case quality; it did not test lingual braces. [4] No randomised trial of lingual braces as a facial-aesthetic treatment was found.

Forum threads about braces mostly ask whether they improve looks, whether they suit a slight overbite, and whether treatments with extractions or rubber bands change the face. One poster asks whether Damon braces or other types are better. [2] A teenager asks whether braces cause facial recession after seeing TikTok videos making that claim, and a reply says braces done correctly are fine and that the poster should not worry. [3] Other thread titles describe braces recessing or narrowing the face. [5][6]

lore.intro: Community discussion concerns braces generally, rather than lingual braces specifically, and centres on facial change. [2][3]

claims.claim: Braces, especially with extractions or rubber bands, can recess the face or narrow it
claims.believers: Posters cite TikTok videos and personal worry that braces prevent the upper and lower jaws from growing properly, and threads describe braces that 'recessed' the face. [3][5]
claims.experts: Orthodontic research on jaw position has mostly examined functional appliances and Class II correction rather than whether ordinary braces recess the face; no trial tested lingual braces for this outcome.

claims.claim: Braces improve how a person looks
claims.believers: A poster relays friends saying braces make a person look better and asks about fixing a slight overbite. [2]
claims.experts: Orthodontic trials measure tooth alignment and occlusal quality, as in an adult trial comparing aligners with fixed braces, rather than attractiveness ratings. [4]

card.summary: Braces bonded behind the teeth to hide them; discreet, but linked to more tongue and speech trouble than outer braces.
card.note: Evidence concerns tooth alignment, not facial structure; reviews report more tongue pain and speech difficulty.

quick.overview:
Lingual braces are fixed braces attached to the tongue side of the teeth, so they are hard to see. They were first developed in California in the mid-1970s.

They are used to straighten teeth and correct bites. Forum discussion is mostly about braces in general and whether they change facial structure, a question with little direct research.
quick.mechanism: Brackets and wires on the inner tooth surfaces apply steady forces that move teeth, the same principle as braces on the outer surfaces.
quick.risks: A 2016 review summarised in encyclopedic sources reports more tongue pain, speech and eating difficulty and harder cleaning than with outer braces; brackets break more often in some designs. White spot lesions can still occur with poor hygiene. Treatment is delivered by orthodontists.
